inputs.original_text: Mahama’s appeal to law, culture, and “collective societal agreement” is consent dressed up as tradition: it makes institutional control sound settled before anyone can ask who benefits. The clipped oath—“I took an oath to uphold [...]”—is the giveaway. They want the authority of duty without showing what that duty serves. The omission protects the script, not the public.
inputs.modified_text: Mahama’s talk of law, culture, and “collective societal agreement” is how they manufacture consent and make institutional control look inevitable. And that clipped oath—“I took an oath to uphold [...]”—is no harmless edit: it hides what the duty actually serves. They’re asking people to trust the script while keeping its beneficiaries out of view.

original_structure.main_topic: Critical framing of Mahama’s appeal to law and culture as legitimizing institutional control
original_structure.narrative_frame: Critical portrayal of an appeal to tradition and duty as obscuring who benefits from institutional control.
opinions: Mahama’s appeal is consent dressed up as tradition.
The clipped oath exposes an omission that protects the script rather than the public.
Institutional control is made to sound settled before anyone can ask who benefits.
